{"id": "8e1a8197-4a03-4910-b6ee-bdcd8269c907", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Good question — these are two of the main load balancer types under AWS Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), and they operate at different layers of the network stack:

**Application Load Balancer (ALB)**
- Operates at Layer 7 (application layer / HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC)
- Routes based on request content — URL path, host header, HTTP method, query strings, headers, etc.
- Supports advanced routing: path-based and host-based routing, redirects, fixed responses
- Great for microservices, container-based apps (ECS/EKS), and anything needing content-aware routing
- Supports WebSockets and HTTP/2
- Can perform authentication (via Cognito or OIDC) at the load balancer

**Network Load Balancer (NLB)**
- Operates at Layer 4 (transport layer / TCP, UDP, TLS)
- Routes purely based on IP protocol data — doesn't inspect request content
- Built for extreme performance: handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency
- Supports static IP addresses per Availability Zone (and Elastic IP assignment) — useful when clients need a fixed IP
- Preserves the source IP of the client by default
- Good fit for latency-sensitive apps, non-HTTP protocols, or when you need a static entry point (e.g., PrivateLink endpoint services)

**In short:** ALB is the smart, content-aware router for web applications; NLB is the fast, low-level router for raw TCP/UDP traffic where performance and static IPs matter more than content-based routing.

Let me know if you'd like help deciding which one fits a specific workload you're running, or if you want to check which type your existing load balancers are using.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
